Kabir is designing a school website. The colour of the heading is written as the hexadecimal code #3DBA5C, where the first two digits give the red value, the next two the green value and the last two the blue value.
(i) Why do designers prefer hexadecimal over binary for such codes? (1)
(ii) Find the decimal value of each of red, green and blue. (2)
(iii) Write the blue value in binary. (1)
items.answer: (i) Each hexadecimal digit stands for 4 bits, so the code is short and easy to read. (ii) red = 61, green = 186, blue = 92 (iii) 01011100
items.markingKey: 1 + 2 + 1 marks: (ii) e.g. 3D = 3×16 + 13 = 61; (iii) each hexadecimal digit as 4 bits: 5 = 0101, C = 1100.

items.stem:
Study the extract below and answer the questions.
"Octal to hexadecimal conversion can be done through binary. Some decimal fractions, such as 0.1, do not have an exact finite binary equivalent. The positional values after the binary point are 2^-1, 2^-2, 2^-3 and so on. The decimal value of a number in any base is the sum of each digit times its positional value."
(i) Explain the term 'repeated multiplication method', which is related to the theme of the extract. (1)
(ii) Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain the following: 0.5 in decimal is exactly 0.1 in binary. (1)
(iii) A student concludes: "Every decimal fraction has an exact finite binary equivalent." Use your knowledge of the chapter to evaluate this conclusion. (2)
items.answer: (i) The method of converting a decimal fraction to another base by multiplying by the base and taking the integer parts in order. (ii) The first place after the binary point has the value 2^-1 = 0.5. (iii) The conclusion is wrong: Fractions such as 0.1 give a repeating binary fraction.
items.markingKey: 1+1+2 marks: (i) The method of converting a decimal fraction to another base by multiplying by the base and taking the integer parts in order. (ii) The first place after the binary point has the value 2^-1 = 0.5. (iii) The conclusion is wrong: Fractions such as 0.1 give a repeating binary fraction.
